analysis.body:
Federal agencies have begun deploying AI across a range of operational tasks, but the adoption landscape remains nascent and fragmented. Per the GAO, twenty of twenty-three agencies reported approximately 1,200 current and planned artificial intelligence use cases, with NASA and the Department of Commerce reporting the highest numbers. Specific applications include analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, analyzing photographs from drones, and targeting of scientific specimens for planetary rovers. However, most of these reported use cases were in the planning phase rather than in production, with only about 200 instances in which agencies reported currently using AI. This gap between planned and operational deployment suggests government AI remains largely exploratory.

The readiness to manage this expansion unevenly distributed across the federal system. Per the GAO, ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. Commerce and the General Services Administration achieved fuller compliance by creating a plan to develop AI technical standards and establishing the AI Center of Excellence, respectively. By contrast, the Offices of Management and Budget and Personnel Management did not fully implement selected requirements, with OMB failing to develop government-wide guidance on how agencies should acquire and use AI and OPM not yet establishing or updating an occupational category for employees performing AI work. The Office of Science and Technology Policy did not communicate its designation of which agencies were expected to fulfill specific AI requirements, adding to the fragmentation.

Data quality and inventory accuracy present immediate operational constraints. Per the GAO, five agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their reported use cases while the other fifteen had instances of incomplete and inaccurate data, with some inventories missing required data elements such as the AI life cycle stage or indication of whether a use case was releasable. Two inventories included AI uses that were later determined by the agencies to not be AI. Without accurate inventories, the government's management of its use of AI will be hindered by incomplete and inaccurate data, limiting visibility into actual spending and risk exposure.

Regulatory infrastructure and legislative activity are accelerating. The AI Laws section of this site tracks 4,343 AI bills across fifty-three jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan, indicating rapid state and federal legislative movement. The OECD.AI platform tracks over 900 national AI policies and initiatives, while Oxford Insights ranks national readiness on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption across nearly every country. Stanford HAI's annual AI Index carries the government and policy track, including legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement trends. This growth in measurement and policy infrastructure reflects recognition that without consistent frameworks, agencies cannot effectively address AI risks and benefits.

Investment in federal AI research and development remains limited relative to potential. Per the GAO, the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included $1.8 billion for nondefense research and development investment in AI. Some agencies are using AI operationally to identify information security threats and facilitate the review of large datasets. Federal agencies can use AI to improve government operations and analyze large datasets, yet safeguards are needed to manage AI risks. Until all federal requirements are met and government-wide guidance on acquisition and use is developed, agencies will continue to operate without consistent risk management or comparative visibility into their deployments.
